title: Holy company
hookLine: Sikhs stress the company of the good

cards: Shoes off at the door. Head covered. Inside a gurdwara, people sit on the carpeted floor facing the Guru Granth Sahib.
A banker sits beside a taxi driver. A grandmother sits beside a student straight from the gym. Nobody has a better seat.

Later, in the kitchen hall, they sit again in rows on the floor, served the same simple meal by volunteers who may have sat beside them an hour ago. Who you sat with matters here, maybe more than how long you stayed.
Sikhs have a word for the people in that room, and for what being among them does to a person.

teach.b: The word is sangat: company, the gathering, the congregation. At a gurdwara, the sangat is everyone who has come: the singers, the cooks, the visitors, you.

teach.h: SADH SANGAT: THE COMPANY OF THE HOLY.
teach.b: Sikhs speak of the sadh sangat, the company of the holy, and the Guru Granth Sahib praises it. One whole section of the Sukhmani Sahib, a long hymn by Guru Arjan, praises that company line after line.
In plain paraphrase: in the company of the holy, the face grows bright, the dirt on the mind is washed away, pride falls off, and the Name of God comes easily. Notice the claim.
Not only that good people are pleasant to be around, but that company changes you. You become, a little, like the people you sit with. So for Sikhs, choosing your company isn't a social detail.
It's part of the practice, like rising early or singing the hymns.

teach.h: A BODY YOU JOIN, NOT A CROWD YOU WATCH.
teach.b: And the sangat isn't a crowd you watch. It's a body you join. You sing with it, cook with it, sweep with it, sit in its rows to eat.
The word travels beyond the gurdwara, too. A family might say the sangat helped them through a funeral. A visitor might hear: the sangat is your family now.
Strip away the language and the question is plain, and sharp. Whose company makes you more patient, more honest, more like the person you mean to be? And whose quietly pulls the other way?

teach.h: COME AND SIT WITH THE SANGAT.
teach.b: Sikhs answer the first part with a place and a people: come and sit with the sangat.

how: Sikhs gather as the sangat at the gurdwara to hear and sing the Guru Granth Sahib, then sit together in rows to share langar, a free meal served by volunteers; keeping good company is treated as part of spiritual life.

the company, the gathering of a congregation

games.q: you visit a gurdwara for the first time and feel like an outsider. you're unsure whether to stay for the meal. what does the tradition invite?
o: sit in the rows and eat with the sangat.
wait until you're a member first.
games.why: the sangat is a body you join, not a crowd you watch. visitors sit and eat in the same rows as everyone else.

practice: Bring to mind one person in whose company you become a little better: kinder, calmer, more honest. Hold their face for a moment, and notice what changes in you as you picture sitting beside them.
If you pray, give thanks for them; if you don't, simply be glad they exist.

wordCard.voice: Sangat. The company, the congregation, in the Sikh tradition. Sadh sangat is the company of the holy, the people whose presence washes the mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the company, the congregation.

carryVoice: Your line: good company. In that room, nobody has a better seat. Until tomorrow.
